replying_to: Replying to Interpreting Black-boxes Using Primitive Parameterized Functions
display_title: Official Review of Paper1334 by Reviewer gBvW

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors propose a method to perform symbolic regression (SR) through a blend of Genetic Programming (GP), the Kolmogorov Superposition Theorem (KST) and gradient optimization. The aim of their method is to develop a black-box interpretation methodology, by approximating black-box models' behavior through their particular flavor of SR. Authors claim that their approach always yields interpretable models, because it relies on a small set of simple, but somehow enough, functions from which symbolic expressions (that adhere to the functional form of KST) are built. Authors test their approach in three different contexts against a set of other symbolic approximation methods, most of them also geared towards black-box interpretation.
content.main_review:
The paper is, in general, well written and organized. Language is clear most of the times. Maybe math notation is overused in some places, but other than that, the paper is easy to follow and understand.

The approach proposed by the authors is novel, such that I consider it worthy of acceptance in that regard. The empirical assessment, on the other hand, is not thorough enough, which makes it difficult for me to reach an overall recommendation rating.

One way or another, there are some points that require clarification in the draft, before I can fully recommend its acceptance. I will enumerate them in order, from what I consider the highest priority, to the lowest:

i. Incorporating _tunable_ coefficients into GP trees is nothing new. Please describe your algorithm in proper terms, such as "memetic algorithm", "local search enhanced GP", etc. with the corresponding references.  And being a _nature-inspired_, evolutionary algorithm, as it is, in GP literature there have been attempts at defining a taxonomy for these kind of algorithms, _Lamarckian_ or _Baldwinian_. Please specify the type of inheritance system used by your approach (_Lamarckian_ I believe), and how such decision could affect the performance of your method. Refer to [1] for more information.

ii. In Sec. 6, authors specify that their approach is computationally more efficient than Symbolic Pursuit (SP); but there is no mention regarding the other baselines they compared against (vanilla GP and Symbolic Metamodeling (SM)). Please remark -if that is the case- that your approach and both of those other methods were given the same computational resources (exec. time-CPU threads). If that is not the case, and either of those methods were given less amount of resources, then results would be meaningless.

iii. The major problem I see with the paper is the experimental study. The whole idea behind KST is to approximate high dimensional functions through a sum of single-variable ones. Therefore, I'd have expected authors to provide an ablation study regarding the dimensionality of the problem being approximated, in the search for evidence that the proposed methods achieves better results than conventional GP or other regression methods, when faced with increasingly higher dimensional problems. Authors could assemble a battery of different, toy-artificial, symbolic regression problems, such as the ones used in Sec. 5.1, but with different number of input variables, say 4, 6, 8, 10, with five problems for each problem size, and then study how each method's performance degrade over higher dimensional problems. I'd would expect that their proposed approach, which performs a more "organized" search (thanks to the KST) could be more resilient to higher dimensional problems (i.e. achieve better results, given the same computational resources).

IV. I think the procedure or intuition for selecting  $l_1$ and $l_2$ is crucial, and should be bring upfront to the main text, not just casually mentioned in the appendices. If I understood correctly, neither crossover nor mutation have the ability to increase the number of middle nodes, thus the importance of such parameters.


1. Emigdio, Z., Trujillo, L., Schütze, O., & Legrand, P. (2014). Evaluating the effects of local search in genetic programming. In EVOLVE-A Bridge between Probability, Set Oriented Numerics, and Evolutionary Computation V (pp. 213-228). Springer, Cham.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper is well written and the proposed approach is properly framed within its aimed scope (blackbox interpretability).
The proposed method is novel and interesting enough to deserve publication. The intuition and motivations behind it are clearly explained through the draft.
The experimental assessment is lacking and sparse. I'd recommend authors to discard study from Sec. 5.2 which is kind of redundant with the other two studies, and instead focus on increasing experimental evidence for sections 5.1 and 5.3.
I may improve my score if some missing definitions and references are properly cited (see point (i) of my complete review).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.details_of_ethics_concerns: No ethics concerns raised my attention during this review.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1334 by Reviewer gBvW

content.title: Responses to reviewer gBvW
content.comment:
Many thanks for your thorough assessment and very insightful comments. In the following we respond to each of the four raised concerns:

1- Thank you for introducing reference [1]. The reason that this is not highlighted in the paper is that we initially were not attempting to propose a new GP method and simply wanted to propose a method based on a better approximation of KST (as described in the paper). The use of GP for optimization of the resulting model was simply a natural solution for the problem we had. However, the resulting method is indeed interesting as a GP approach. As you mentioned our method is a memetic algorithm and is also Lamarckian. As also highlighted in [1] the area of using GD or other refinement methods is understudied and there are few methods that are attempting to do this. In particular, only GP methods that use gradient descent, using GD only for tuning of numerical constants. From this perspective, I think our proposed method can be very interesting as a new method that uses gradient descent also for tuning the primitive functions (building blocks). We have highlighted this aspect of this work in the revised version (please see blue sections of introduction and Section 2), we also added a few relevant citations.

2- Yes, we run all the simulations on a personal laptop with the same allocated resources. We have clarified this in the revised version. The reason that we focused only on SP was that it was the only method that was competitive with our method and other baselines were not performing well enough. 

3- Thank you for this suggestion. We have implemented your suggested experiment and reported it in the appendix (please see the blue section of Appendix E and Table 7). In short, we found that our method is the most robust one, and we actually found anomalies in SP and SR. E.g. the performance of SP dramatically changes with the random seed, and the difference of training and test error of SR can be very large which resulted in poor performance.


4- This is a correct observation. l_1 and l_2 are indeed important hyperparameters. We have highlighted this in Section 3. 

Regarding, experiment 5.2, we also think it is a good suggestion to push it to the appendix and replace it with the extension of experiment 5.1. This needs to rewriting section 5.1 which did not have time for, but we can do this in the final version. We hope that we have addressed all of the raised concerns, we are happy to provide additional results if needed.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1334 by Reviewer ir7c

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an algorithm for approximating general multivariate functions. With this approximation, the authors aim at approximating a trained (black-box) machine learning model and use their approximation for interpretation.  The algorithm produces a composition of univariate simple parameterized functions. This composition is selected from a collection of tree configurations each of which represents different relations between primitive functions and the variables (features). The parameters of the univariate functions used in each tree are obtained by gradient descent (training phase). As for selecting the best tree, a variant of genetic algorithms is applied. The authors have also compared their algorithm against other methods from the literature on a set of synthetic and standard data sets.
content.main_review:
The manuscript is clearly written, and the approach is interesting. However, I have had difficulties in assessing its novelty, particularly along the following lines:

1) The authors aim at giving an interpretation to a black-box model. However, their approach seems only a function approximation method (methods similar to theirs have already appeared in the literature). I do not see, how using simple parameterized functions (even though they are provided by the domain experts) in the approximation makes their method more interpretable? Take for instance the final model in Section 5.1. The resulting expression is highly nonlinear, and hence, difficult to interpret. Overall, I would appreciate if authors can provide clarification about "interpretability" gained with their approach. 

2) The authors are trying to approximate a trained model by solving (2). Can one also use the similar steps to come up with a new machine learning algorithm by solving $$\min_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \sum_i \ell(g(\mathbf{x}_i) - y_i),$$ where $g$ is defined in (5). If this would work and the resulting model is considered to be interpretable, then would we obtain a new inherently interpretable machine learning approach?

3) The proposed algorithm uses many hyper-parameters. In addition to difficulties with tuning them, these parameters also raise a concern about the robustness of the resulting models. If we change the data or the parameters slightly, how would the resulting model obtained with the proposed approach change?

4) Does Kolmogorov superposition theorem (KST) work when we specify the set $\mathcal{G}$? In other words, when the user selects several simple parametric functions, can we guarantee that KST still holds?

5) In the last section, and also in a few other places including the appendix, the authors state that they can use more complex functions and trees to approximate certain black-box models. Then, how would this affect the interpretability of the resulting model from your approach?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper may have a potential, but in its current state it does not provide convincing arguments about its novelty and its major claim about the interpretability of the proposed approach.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1334 by Reviewer ir7c

content.title: Responses to reviewer ir7c
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed review and insightful comments.

1- This seems to be a general comment about all metamodeling approaches for interpretation (e.g. SM and SP). As discussed in section 3.3, there are several ways that a metamodel can provide interpretations: instance-wise feature importance, feature interactions, and also functional form. In section 5.1, for example, the metamodel correctly identifies the exponential form of the black box. This can potentially be a piece of very valuable information for a domain expert. Assume that the data is collected from a physical experiment and this method is used to identify the underlying relations, here we correctly identified the exponential nature of the problem which can be valuable to domain experts (this way of using our method is exactly what you are suggesting in your next comment). Since you mention the non-linearity of the found model we should clarify that metamodels are “global approximations”, hence they are expected to be highly non-linear. If a local linear approximation is required we can simply consider the first-order Taylor expansion of these functions in the point of interest.


2- This is a correct observation (also mentioned by reviewer eUVj and in fact reviewers of SM and SP papers). There are two reasons for why we are using the black-box for training and not  directly using dataset. One is that from the user point of view we may have been given a task of interpreting a black-box, i.e., the user’s question may be why this particular method is working, and not necessarily looking for another interpretable model. 2- More importantly, we may not have access to the dataset for various reasons including privacy concerns. In this method we only need querying the black-box method and we can use random inputs. Having said that, directly using dataset in all symbolic metamodeling methods as you have suggested is certainly possible and relevant. In the revision version, we have clarified this important point in the discussion section. 

3- In the appendix, we have provided results to show that our performance is not particularly related to the choice of primitive functions. Several of hyperparameters are trade off between performance and complexity, e.g., M number of trees in each generation or maximum number of iterations. We have not observed a significant reliance on the choice of hyperparameters, this is reflected in the fact that we used similar hyperparameters in all experiments as reported in the appendix.


4- For KST to hold, as stated in the theorem 1, G should be the class of all continuous functions. Here (similar to all symbolic models), we aim for an approximation, note that technically the black box itself is an approximation of the underlying function. From another perspective, most of natural mechanisms, think of physics laws, are expected to be expressed with smooth functions. Thus, using our parameterized functions as an approximation can be useful. Furthermore, our experiments confirm that our method can find acceptable approximations.

5- Firstly, as we have mentioned in the paper there are several ways of providing interpretations including feature importance, or feature interactions that can be estimated by computing Taylor expansion, thus the functional form is not the only method of interpretation that we are suggesting here. As you suggested, using more layers (proposed as a possibility in the appendix) will make the resulting metamodel more complex, and hence inspecting it will be less informative. This is a trade-off, by using more layers we can construct more complicated metamodels which can potentially approximate black boxes better, but we are losing the simplicity of the expression of metamodel in return. This is actually relevant to your point 4, if we were using general functions then there was no need to use trees with more than three layers, as KST guarantees the existence of suitable functions. However, using simple functions may not be suitable for some problems in which we can either use more layers or use more complicated primitive functions (e.g., Meijer G functions).

In response to reviewer gBvW, we have added an additional experiment (please see the blue section of the appendix in the revised version) comparing the performance of different methods when adding the number of variables to the synthetic function, this experiment further shows the robustness of our method comparing to our competitors. We are willing to provide additional explanations/experiments if needed and would appreciate it if you can reevaluate your score given these responses.

replying_to: Replying to Interpreting Black-boxes Using Primitive Parameterized Functions
display_title: Official Review of Paper1334 by Reviewer eUVj

content.summary_of_the_paper: Following several recent works, the paper proposes to learn an interpretable proxy (called a symbolic metamodel) of a black-box ML model. This proxy can then be used for its intrinsic interpretability or for deriving local or global feature rankings. The originality of the approach lies in the way the metamodel is defined and trained. A two-level tree is used to represent mathematical expressions (motivated by Kolmogorov's superposition theorem) that combine simple univariate primitive parameterized functions. The metamodel is trained by combining gradient descent to tune the parameters of the primitive functions and genetic programming to learn the tree structure. The approach, called SMPF ("symbolic metamodeling using primitive functions") is compared empirically against several related methods.
content.main_review:
The topic is highly relevant and timely. The paper is well written and easy too follow.

The novelty of the approach is limited with respect to the SM and SP methods papers, i.e., (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2019) and (Crabble et al, 2020). The general idea of the approach (training a symbolic metamodel, whose structure is inspired by Kolmogorov's superposition theorem) is similar in all three works. The novelty here is how the metamodel is parameterized (using a subset of predefined parameterized primitive functions) and how it is trained (using a mix of gradient descent and genetic programming).The algorithm is globally sound but it is not very original with respect to existing symbolic regression methods based also on genetic programming.

The main limitation of the paper is that the authors do not really convincingly show that the modifications are important with respect to SM, SP and SR. The experiments focus almost exclusively on the evaluation of the predictive performance of the different metamodels and not really on their benefit in terms of interpretability, which is the main incentive for these methods (see my detailed comments below). 

Another limitation of the algorithm is the fact that it introduces a lot of new hyper-parameters, including the choice of the primitive functions. The impact of these hyper-parameters is not really assessed in the paper and they were furthermore set differently in all three experiments, suggesting that setting them properly is crucial. This is an important drawback in practice, especially for a method that is supposed to bring explainability.

The general idea of training a surrogate symbolic metamodels to explain a black-box is an interesting idea in general. But actually, I don't see why the black-box model is needed here. From what I understand from the experiment on the real dataset (Section 5.3), the black-box is only used to provide new output values for the existing training set examples and thus it would be possible to train the SMPF metamodel directly from the original data. Why is then the approach branded as a post-hoc interpretation method and not as an intrinsically interpretable model? Is there any benefit in terms of predictive performance or interpretability to train from the black-box predictions? I know that this comment applies also to the SM and SP methods, but my feeling is that the paper should answer this question.

Overall, the specific implementation proposed in the paper is interesting and it has a clear potential with respect to SP and SM but I think that, for a third paper on this topic, the experimental part should have been stronger to really highlight the improvement in terms of interpretability with respect to previous works.

Detailed comments:

- In Experiment 1, the authors claim that SMPF has a better accuracy than the other methods and is able to identify the functional form in most cases but actually no results are provided, neither in the paper, nor in the appendices (although results are provided for other sets of function in Table 4 and more complex functions in E.1). We have to trust the authors that it's really the case.
- Despite the focus on interpretability, no symbolic metamodel is shown, except one in 5.1. In this specific example, why is the model produced considered satisfactory? It looks much more complex than the original model (despite the fact that the choice of primitive functions is ideal). One needs also to show metamodels produced by the other methods for comparison (only one model produced by SP is shown in 5.1). In particular, I'm curious to see what kind of formulas are produced by SR, which is the most flexible method.
- In Section 3.3, the authors claim that inspection of survived trees could be informative, in particular to highlight interactions between variables. Again, this possibility is not illustrated in the experiments.
- I know that the idea of the experiment in 5.2 comes from (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2019) but I don't find this experiment very relevant. Computing instance-wise feature importance with partial derivatives of the metamodel does not make sense when it is possible to compute these partial derivatives directly from the original black-box model, which is the case with neural networks. At the very least, feature importances derived directly from the black-box should be compared to the one derived from the metamodel.
- Results in Figure 3 are inconsistent with the results in (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2019). For example, L2X is the best method on the XOR problem in (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2019), while it fails here. The same difference appears in the case of DeepLIFT on the nonlinear additive problem.
- The text in 5.2 says "we find the median feature importance ranking". Do you mean the median feature importance ranking of the relevant feature on each problem (because the median feature importance ranking over all features is a constant)? I think that they are irrelevant features on these problems that should ideally not be selected in the black-box model. This should be checked.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the specific implementation proposed in the paper is interesting and it has a clear potential with respect to related works but I think that the experimental part should have been stronger to really highlight the improvement in terms of interpretability with respect to previous works.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.

content.title: Responses to reviewer eUVj
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed and insightful comments. 

- Regarding novelty: in addition to what you mentioned (i.e., the introduction of primitive functions and using GP and GD for training), we think that our new method of approximating KST is one of the main novelties here (e.g. note that comparing SP and SM, the only novelty of SP is a new approximation of KST). Our better and more general approximation of KST allowed us to use simpler functions (compared to Meijer G-functions) and have a more flexible framework (we can use any parameterized function as primitive functions). Here we also connect KST to GP type algorithm via our tree representation, the resulting method can be classified as a memetic algorithm in GP literature. Previously, gradient descent has been used only for tuning the numerical constants in GP methods, here we are using it for tuning building blocks as well which is the first of its kind.

- About using the same set of primitive functions and the concern that the performance may be very dependent on this particular set, we have provided results of some other sets of primitive functions in Appendix C exactly to show that this is not the case.

- About the use of black-box vs directly using training data: This is a correct observation (also mentioned by reviewer ir7c and in fact reviewers of SM and SP papers). There are two reasons why we are using the black box for training and not directly using the dataset. One is that from the user point of view we may have been given a task of interpreting a black-box, i.e., the user’s question may be why this particular method is working, and not necessarily looking for another interpretable model. 2- More importantly, we may not have access to the dataset for various reasons including privacy concerns. In this method, we only need to query the black-box and we can use random inputs (as many of them as we want). Having said that, directly using the dataset in all symbolic metamodeling methods as you have suggested is certainly possible and relevant. In the revised version, we have clarified this important point in the discussion section. 


Detailed comments:

1- It seems that you have not seen Table 1 which was printed on page 7 (a page before section 5.1). In the revision version Table 1 is on the same page as the start of Section 5.1. Also, we added a reference to this Table in the explanation of experiment 1 to avoid confusion.

2- Note that “the original model” is a black box and is not known. Therefore, suggesting exponential function or sin function as in experiment 1 is significantly valuable information. Assume that this data is generated from a physical experiment for which we do not know the formula, then knowing the functional form can be very helpful. We show the expression of SP for one example, the result of SP for the other three functions are similarly can only be expressed in form of Meijer G-functions. This is also the case for SM. (SP^p which is Taylor's approximation of SP is obviously a polynomial). Regarding SR, for example for the sin function of experiment 1 X0*X1 is the found metamodel.

3- We concede that we have not shown this in the experiments, this was more of a suggestion for future work, we have modified that section accordingly in the revised version to accurately reflect our position.

4- As you mentioned we are here replicating the exact setup suggested in (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2019) to be able to compare our methods. As far as we know, computing the partial derivatives with respect to features is not trivial, if you think there is a particular method that needs to be added to the set of methods in this experiment, we are happy to add that if you point us to the relevant reference.

5- For this experiment, we are using the code provided at https://github.com/ahmedmalaa/Symbolic-Metamodeling. We have noticed this difference, but we could not find why, we also did try reaching to authors but it was not successful. It should be mentioned that even assuming that the result reported in (Alaa & van der Schaar, 2019) is correct will not dramatically change the general message of this experiment.

6- Yes, we meant the median rank of “relevant” features. We have corrected this sentence.

In response to reviewer gBvW, we have added an additional experiment (please see the blue section of the appendix in the revised version) comparing the performance of different methods when adding the number of variables to the synthetic function, this experiment further shows the robustness of our method compared to our competitors. We are willing to provide additional explanation/experiments if needed and would appreciate it if you can reevaluate your score given these responses

display_title: Official Review of Paper1334 by Reviewer zK8e

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The main premise of the paper is that building a (global) approximation a black box model using simple interpretable functions results in a model which is more useful for the purpose of interpretability. In particular, the resulting approximation is useful for 1) understanding feature importances 2) analyzing feature interactions and 3) scientific discovery by revealing underlying laws governing the observed data


Their approach is based on the Kolmogorov superposition theorem, and results in a multilayer network (which they call a tree) formed from the composition of primitive parametrized univariate functions. This is learnt using a combination of gradient descent (for optimizing the parameters) and genetic programming (for searching over tree configurations).

They show experimentally that their approach results in reasonable approximations.
content.main_review:
My main concern about this paper is that the main premise (that the  approximation results in better interpretability) is not justified. While they discuss how various applications (such as clinical applications) require interpretable models, they do not actually show that the resulting "tree" is interpretable by clinicians (or even other ML researchers). Incorporating simple functions into a multi-layer network does not necessarily preserve the simplicity/interpretability of the primitive functions. Even when restricted to just ranking features by importance, it was hard to see if their approach was significantly better than other approaches. 
The process of generating the approximation is based on GP/GD - it is unclear how effective this is. Does this process "overfit" in that it results in more complicated (and less interpretable) solutions if allowed to take arbitrary computational resources? Is the regularization term (lambda E) effective in producing more intepretable models ?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, its not clear that the paper is proposing a mechanism that results in significantly interpretable models, nor does the GP/GD procedure proposed seem to be sufficiently important / novel to justify publication on its own.

content.title: Responses to reviewer zK8e
content.comment:
Thank you for your insightful comments.

Regarding usability of our method: This seems to be a general comment about all metamodeling approaches (i.e. SM and SP) and not particularly our method. There are several ways that a metamodel can provide interpretations: instance-wise feature importance, feature interactions, and also functional form. How much this is helpful for e.g. a clinician is a debatable question and probably depends on the individual. Observing the mathematical expression of the model can potentially increase the trust of a clinician. However, this is not the only way this method can be used. In section 5.1, for example, the metamodel correctly identifies the exponential form of the black box. This can potentially be very valuable information for a domain expert, E.g. see [1]. Assume that the data is collected from a physical experiment and this method is used to identify the underlying governing, here we correctly identified the exponential nature of the problem.

Regarding the complexity of metamodel expression: note that we are proposing a global approximation, therefore expecting that we end up with a simple function is unrealistic. If our global approximation is too complex for the domain expert (these definitions are not clear and different individuals may have different opinions) one can inspect local approximations of the metamodel instead.

“The process of generating the approximation is based on GP/GD - it is unclear how effective this is.” We have provided the results of several experiments to show the effectiveness of our method. In terms of the combination of GP/GD, this method can be classified as memetic algorithms which are using population-based methods paired with other refinement methods (in our case gradient descent). This is an understudied area (see [2]), and there are few methods that are attempting to do this. In particular, only GP methods that use gradient descent, using GD only for tuning of numerical constants. From this perspective, our proposed method can be very interesting as a new method that uses gradient descent also for tuning the primitive functions (building blocks). We have highlighted this aspect of this work in the revised version (please see the blue sections of the introduction and Section 2).

Regarding overfitting, our training and test losses were close enough in the experiments that we ran. In fact, we have shown in experiment 3, that our method actually can regularize the black-box, as we use simple, smooth functions. We also discussed this in the additional experiment (blue section of appendix in revised version). However, our method may overfit, if one uses an arbitrarily large number of middle nodes (outer functions). 

1. Udrescu, S. M., & Tegmark, M. (2020). AI Feynman: A physics-inspired method for symbolic regression. Science Advances, 6(16), eaay2631.
2. Emigdio, Z., Trujillo, L., Schütze, O., & Legrand, P. (2014). Evaluating the effects of local search in genetic programming. In EVOLVE-A Bridge between Probability, Set Oriented Numerics, and Evolutionary Computation V (pp. 213-228). Springer, Cham.
